title: Identity systems — Image Wiki
text:
Identity systems
  The set of decisions that make a mark work everywhere — colour, typeface, grid, formats, signage, artwork masters and the rules about who may change what. Its real purpose is governance, not beauty.

  
    Termvisual identity system / graphic standards
    Also calledbrand guidelines, graphic standards manual, design system, style guide
    Not the same aslogo, brand, house style
    Read8 min
  

  
    
      On this page
      
        What a system adds that a mark cannotThe escape hatch, and what it costsThe unglamorous middle of the manualThe real subject is governanceCommon mistakes
      
    
  

  Pick up a US national park brochure. Then pick up one from a different park, two thousand miles away, about a completely different subject — zooplankton instead of atomic history. They match. Same panel size, same black band, same folds, same type.
There are over 400 parks handing these out, roughly 20 million copies a year, and no single person designs them. What holds them together is a system the National Park Service commissioned from Massimo Vignelli in 1977, built on a panel of 4 by 8¼ inches defined by the fold lines, with widths and lengths chosen to cut cleanly out of a standard 25 by 38 inch press sheet (ID-010). Nobody decides the paper. Nobody decides the fold. The designers argue about the map.
That is what a system is for, and the 1985 Presidential Design Award citation said it better than any textbook: the programme "fulfills the primary objective of a design system, reducing routine decisions so that effort can be concentrated on quality" (ID-010).
What a system adds that a mark cannot
A mark alone answers one question: whose is this (What a logo does). A system answers everything that comes after, which is mostly about materials and hands:

Artwork masters — the one file everyone copies, so nobody redraws.
Colour — named, with formulas per process, and rules for which backgrounds are allowed.
Typeface — one family, so a page nobody has seen still looks related.
A grid — a shared understructure for every page size you print.
Formats — stationery, brochure, press kit, poster, app icon, social profile.
Physical applications — signs, vehicles, uniforms, badges, giveaways. NASA's 1976 index has a section each for signage, motor vehicles, vinyl decals and uniform patches.
Governance — who approves, who to ask, and what happens to a variant nobody approved.

The 1976 NASA Graphics Standards Manual is that list made visible, and it starts with the master file.



NASA Graphics Standards Manual, 1976, p. 1.1 (ID-006). A US Government work, so the document itself carries no copyright.
Read the last paragraph. The logotype "must not be re-drawn, but rather reproduced photographically from reproduction artwork included in Section 2 of this manual." In 1976 that instruction was the entire version-control system: Section 2 of the binder holds camera-ready sheets of the mark and the signatures, and a print shop shot them with a camera rather than tracing them.
The reason is in the drawing above it. All four letters are one stroke width, and the cross-strokes are gone from both A's. Any of that redrawn by hand comes back slightly wrong, and slightly wrong, repeated across an agency for a decade, is a different mark.


The escape hatch, and what it costs
A photographic master works up to the size of a camera. Signs are bigger than that, so the manual gives one licensed exception.



NASA Graphics Standards Manual, 1976, p. 1.7 (ID-006). A US Government work, so the document itself carries no copyright.
For large applications such as signage the mark may be rebuilt, but only from this grid, and the manual pins the scale with one number: three grid units equal the vertical stroke width. Count the squares across the upright of the N and you will find three.
That single ratio turns an aesthetic judgement into arithmetic a sign fabricator can execute in a workshop, without the manual, without a designer on the phone. It is also why the page is turned on its side and is mostly grid: the drawing is a tool, not an illustration.


The unglamorous middle of the manual
Two thirds of any real identity manual is not about the mark at all. It is about type, grid, and the ordinary business of telling a reader what to look at first (Visual hierarchy).


Section 5.3: the specified typeface
Section 5.14: the grid method


NASA Graphics Standards Manual, 1976, pp. 5.3 and 5.14 (ID-006). A US Government work, so the document itself carries no copyright.
Left: Helvetica, named as "the most important family of type in the NASA Unified Visual Communications System" — Light for text and for the agency name locked to the logotype, Medium for headings. Below the alphabets are the same paragraph set two ways, which is how you check a specification rather than admire it.
Right: the grid, in three steps. Blank spread, then the two-column structure that fixes every margin, gutter and page number, then the same spread with headline, columns, a photograph and captions dropped into it. The manual's own reason for the grid is not beauty: it "will save countless man hours in execution."


The real subject is governance
Everything above only works if it survives contact with hundreds of people who will never meet the designer. So the durable parts of a system are the boring ones: a named owner, a supply of masters, and a phone number.
Canada's Federal Identity Program did this with stock. Every institution was issued reproduction proofs in the sizes actually used — the Coat of Arms from 12 to 24 mm, the "Canada" wordmark from 20 to 30 mm and again from 35 to 60 mm — and a central office keeps the original artwork for anything larger (ID-009). It also defines its own vocabulary, so that "design standard", "field of application" and "signature" mean one thing in an argument.
The EPA solved the same problem by restricting inventions: programme identifiers other than the agency seal or logo "are discouraged and require approval" from the Office of Public Affairs, and any approved one "must not be so large as to compete with the Agency's identification system" (ID-012). That is a rule about ambition, not about graphics.
GOV.UK is the living version of the same document. Instead of a binder there is a website and a public asset repository, and the spacing rules are expressed in a unit that ships with the artwork: the dot in the wordmark. Clear space is measured in dots, the gap between crown and wordmark is three crown dots, and the crown scales so that the wordmark dot is twice the crown dot — with an enlarged crown for small applications where the standard one would stop reading. Minimum sizes are stated in pixels: 50 px wide for the wordmark, 16 px for the crown, and a separate small crown for anything below that, such as a favicon (ID-013-c6). Nothing about that is decoration. It is the 1976 manual with a different distribution mechanism.

Why the manual is free to read and the mark still is not free to use
Both facts are true at once and they get confused constantly. The 1976 manual is a work of the US federal government, so the document carries no copyright — that is why its pages appear here. The mark itself is a different question: NASA's current brand centre states plainly that the insignia, logotype and identifiers are not in the public domain and are protected under 14 CFR 1221. Copyright is one kind of protection; an official insignia gets another, closer to a trademark. So you may study the pages, and you may not put the worm on a T-shirt. The same split shows up in the UK: the Open Government Licence covers GOV.UK's text and data but explicitly exempts departmental logos, crests and the Royal Arms.

Common mistakes

"We have a logo and a colour, so we have an identity." You have two of seven things. The first unplanned format — a conference banner, an app icon — is where you find out.
"The manual is there to keep design consistent." It is there to keep decisions from being retaken. Consistency is the side effect.
"More rules mean less freedom." The Unigrid is strict about panel, paper and fold, and NPS notes that two brochures of the same size, even by the same designer, may look quite different (ID-010). Constraints were applied to the parts nobody should be spending judgement on.
"A system is a document." A document with no owner, no master files and nobody to ask decays into folklore within two years.


Judging an identity system

Find the mark in three different places. Is it the same mark, or three tracings?
Ask what the unit of measurement is. Real systems measure clear space and spacing in something derived from the mark itself.
Look for the small-size version. If there is only one drawing, the system has not met a favicon yet.
Look at a format nobody thought about: a vehicle door, a lanyard, a spreadsheet header. Does the system reach it?
Ask who says no. If the answer is nobody, you are looking at a mood board.
